{"problem": {"theorem": "Consider a prime $p$ of the form $4 t+3$. Show that $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p$ iff $-a$ has order $(p-1) / 2$.", "assumptions": [], "domain": "number_theory", "proof_text": "\begin{proof}

    Let $a$ a primitive root modulo $p$.

As $a^{p-1} \equiv 1(\bmod p), p \mid\left(a^{(p-1) / 2}-1\right)\left(a^{(p-1) / 2}+1\right)$, so $p \mid a^{(p-1) / 2}-1$ or $p \mid$ $a^{(p-1) / 2}+1$. As $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p, a^{(p-1) / 2} \not \equiv 1(\bmod p)$, so

$$

a^{(p-1) / 2} \equiv-1 \quad(\bmod p) .

$$

Hence $(-a)^{(p-1) / 2}=(-1)^{2 t+1} a^{(p-1) / 2} \equiv(-1) \times(-1)=1(\bmod p)$.

Suppose that $(-a)^n \equiv 1(\bmod p)$, with $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Then $a^{2 n}=(-a)^{2 n} \equiv 1(\bmod p)$, so $p-1\left|2 n, \frac{p-1}{2}\right| n$.

So $-a$ has order $(p-1) / 2$ modulo $p$.

Conversely, suppose that $-a$ has order $(p-1) / 2=2 t+1$ modulo $p$. Let $2, p_1, \ldots p_k$ the prime factors of $p-1$, where $p_i$ are odd.

$a^{(p-1) / 2}=a^{2 t+1}=-(-a)^{2 t+1}=-(-a)^{(p-1) / 2} \equiv-1$, so $a^{(p-1) / 2} \not \equiv 1(\bmod 2)$.

As $p-1$ is even, $(p-1) / p_i$ is even, so $a^{(p-1) / p_i}=(-a)^{(p-1) / p_i} \not \equiv 1(\bmod p)($ since $-a$ has order $p-1)$.

So the order of $a$ is $p-1$ (see Ex. 4.8) : $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p$.

\end{proof}", "explicit_subgoals": []}, "rule_candidates": [{"id": "grp_normal_quotient", "name": "Quotient group criterion", "statement": "If N is a normal subgroup of G, then the set of left cosets G/N forms a group under (aN)(bN) = abN.", "conditions": ["N is a subgroup of G", "N is normal in G"], "conclusion": "G/N is a group and coset multiplication is well-defined.", "rule_digest": "f6d458aa2e7463efeea7a535cdbe0f0f7930259cfe7f845b5350ec03454da876", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "ring_quotient_ideal", "name": "Quotient ring criterion", "statement": "If I is a two-sided ideal of a ring R, then R/I is a quotient ring with operations defined on cosets.", "conditions": ["I is a two-sided ideal of R"], "conclusion": "R/I is a ring and coset operations are well-defined.", "rule_digest": "5c419f063bbc02eba57c0943d5ecce5f2e4c1b370cbb5ad6d69c2e08c3b21835", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "grp_first_iso", "name": "First isomorphism theorem for groups", "statement": "If phi: G -> H is a group homomorphism, then G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "conditions": ["phi is a group homomorphism", "ker(phi) is the kernel of phi"], "conclusion": "G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "rule_digest": "335c687d26f64e41584f1b8bc575aec9d78223b01c4821bf0056bf8533de0c19", "applicability": "unchecked"}]}

{"kind":"proof","text":"Let \(m=(p-1)/2=2t+1\), which is odd, and work in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times\).

Suppose first that \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\). Then \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1=2m\). Since \(a^m\neq1\) but \((a^m)^2=1\), we have \(a^m\equiv-1\pmod p\). Hence
\[
(-a)^m=(-1)^m a^m\equiv(-1)(-1)\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)\mid m\). Conversely, if \((-a)^n\equiv1\pmod p\), then
\[
a^{2n}=(-a)^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Since \(a\) has order \(2m\), this implies \(2m\mid2n\), hence \(m\mid n\). Therefore \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m=(p-1)/2\).

Conversely, suppose \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m\). Put \(b=-a\), so \(a=-b\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(b)=m\). Certainly
\[
a^{2m}=(-b)^{2m}=b^{2m}\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
so \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid2m\). If \(a^n\equiv1\pmod p\), then after squaring we get \(b^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p\). Hence \(m\mid2n\), and because \(m\) is odd, \(m\mid n\). Write \(n=mq\). Since \(b^n\equiv1\),
\[
1\equiv a^n=(-1)^n b^n=(-1)^n,
\]
so \(n\) is even. As \(m\) is odd, \(q\) must be even; therefore \(2m\mid n\). It follows that \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=2m=p-1\), so \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\).","reason":"The argument uses that \((p-1)/2\) is odd and proves both required order equalities directly. It repairs the supplied converse, which incorrectly says that \(-a\) has order \(p-1\) and also contains an erroneous reduction modulo \(2\)."}
